{{Short description|Topological space}}
[[File:Dendrite_julia.png|thumb|right|A [[dendrite (mathematics)|dendrite]] such as this [[Julia set]] is a (locally connected) dendroid.]]
In mathematics, a '''dendroid''' is a type of [[topological space]], satisfying the properties that it is hereditarily [[unicoherent]] (meaning that every [[continuum (topology)|subcontinuum]] of ''X'' is unicoherent), [[Connected space#Path connectedness|arcwise connected]], and forms a [[continuum (topology)|continuum]].<ref name="cook95">{{citation|last=Cook|first=H.|title=Continua: With the Houston Problem Book|volume=170|series=Lecture Notes in Pure and Applied Mathematics|publisher=CRC Press|year=1995|isbn=9780824796501|page=31|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bVcZGMOA4AEC&pg=PA31}}</ref> The term dendroid was introduced by [[Bronisław Knaster]] lecturing at the [[University of Wrocław]],<ref name="charatonik">{{citation
 | last = Charatonik | first = Janusz J.
 | contribution = The works of Bronisław Knaster (1893–1980) in continuum theory
 | location = Dordrecht
 | mr = 1617581
 | pages = 63–78
 | publisher = Kluwer Acad. Publ.
 | title = Handbook of the history of general topology, Vol. 1
 | year = 1997}}.</ref> although these spaces were studied earlier by [[Karol Borsuk]] and others.<ref name="b54">{{citation|first=K.|last=Borsuk|title=A theorem on fixed points|year=1954|journal=Bulletin de l'Académie polonaise des sciences. Classe troisième.|volume=2|pages=17&ndash;20}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|url=http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm49/fm49124.pdf|first=A|last=Lelek|title=On plane dendroids and their end points in the classical sense|journal=Fund. Math.|year=1961|volume=49|issue=3|pages=301&ndash;319|doi=10.4064/fm-49-3-301-319|doi-access=free}}.
</ref>

{{harvtxt|Borsuk|1954}} proved that dendroids have the [[fixed-point theorem|fixed-point property]]: Every continuous function from a dendroid to itself has a fixed point.<ref name="b54"/> {{harvtxt|Cook|1970}} proved that every dendroid is ''tree-like'', meaning that it has arbitrarily fine open covers whose [[Nerve of a covering|nerve]] is a tree.<ref name="cook95"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Cook | first = H.
 | journal = Fundamenta Mathematicae
 | mr = 0261558
 | pages = 19–22
 | title = Tree-likeness of dendroids and λ-dendroids
 | volume = 68
 | year = 1970| doi = 10.4064/fm-68-1-19-22
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> The more general question of whether every tree-like continuum has the fixed-point property, posed by {{harvtxt|Bing|1951}},<ref>{{citation
 | last = Bing | first = R. H. | authorlink = R. H. Bing
 | journal = Duke Mathematical Journal
 | mr = 0043450
 | pages = 653–663
 | title = Snake-like continua
 | volume = 18
 | issue = 3 | year = 1951
 | doi=10.1215/s0012-7094-51-01857-1}}.</ref>
was solved in the negative by David P. Bellamy, who gave an example of a tree-like continuum without the fixed-point property.
<ref>{{citation
 | last = Bellamy | first = David P. 
 | journal = Houston J. Math.
 | mr = 0575909
 | pages = 1–13
 | title = A tree-like continuum without the fixed-point property
 | volume = 6
 | year = 1980}}.</ref>

In Knaster's original publication on dendroids, in 1961, he posed the problem of characterizing the dendroids which can be embedded into the [[Euclidean plane]].  This problem remains open.<ref name="charatonik"/><ref>{{citation|title=Open Problems in Topology II|editor-first=Elliott M.|editor-last=Pearl|publisher=Elsevier|year=2011|isbn=9780080475295|contribution=Open problems on dendroids|first1=Veronica|last1=Martínez-de-la-Vega|author1-link=Verónica Martínez de la Vega|first2=Jorge M.|last2=Martínez-Montejano|pages=319–334}}. See in particular p.&nbsp;331.</ref> Another problem posed in the same year by Knaster, on the existence of an uncountable collection of dendroids with the property that no dendroid in the collection has a continuous [[surjection]] onto any other dendroid in the collection, was solved by {{harvtxt|Minc|2010}} and {{harvtxt|Islas|2007}}, who gave an example of such a family.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Minc | first = Piotr
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Houston Journal of Mathematics
 | mr = 2753740
 | pages = 1185–1205
 | title = An uncountable collection of dendroids mutually incomparable by continuous functions
 | volume = 36
 | year = 2010}}. Previously announced in 2006.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Islas | first = Carlos
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Topology Proceedings
 | mr = 2363160
 | pages = 151–161
 | title = An uncountable collection of mutually incomparable planar fans
 | volume = 31
 | year = 2007}}.</ref>

A locally connected dendroid is called a [[dendrite (mathematics)|dendrite]].  A cone over the [[Cantor set]] (called a Cantor fan) is an example of a dendroid that is not a dendrite.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=J.J.|last1=Charatonik|first2=W.J.|last2=Charatonik|first3=S.|last3=Miklos|title=Confluent mappings of fans|journal=Dissertationes Mathematicae|volume=301|year=1990|pages=1&ndash;86}}</ref>
